title: What is the Texas ratio?
gist: The FRED Blog defines the Texas ratio — a bank's nonperforming loans over tangible equity plus loan-loss reserves, devised by Gerard Cassidy during the 1980s Texas oil-and-real-estate banking crisis — and shows the aggregate for all FDIC-insured US commercial banks at 5.82%, near the 4.59% all-time low of Q2 2022. Above 100% flags a bank whose bad loans exceed its entire loss cushion.

insights.claim: The Texas ratio is a bank credit-risk metric equal to nonperforming loans divided by the sum of tangible equity capital and the allowance for losses on loans and leases.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Gives a single, reproducible screen for whether a bank's loss cushion can absorb its bad loans, usable across any bank with call-report data.
insights.quote: The Texas ratio measures a bank’s nonperforming loans divided by the sum of tangible equity capital and allowance for losses on loans and leases.

insights.claim: The numerator of the Texas ratio counts three distinct categories of trouble: nonaccrual loans, loans 90 or more days past due, and real estate acquired through foreclosure (other real estate owned).
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
entities: Real estate assets acquired through foreclosure
insights.so_what: Screens that ignore OREO or 90-day-past-due balances understate stress; check which components a published bank ratio actually includes before comparing lenders.

insights.claim: Tangible equity capital in the Texas ratio is total bank equity capital less intangible assets, so goodwill-heavy balance sheets get no credit for their loss-absorbing cushion.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Acquisitive banks carrying large goodwill will screen worse on this metric than headline equity ratios suggest — a deliberate conservatism worth replicating in your own screens.
insights.quote: Tangible equity capital represents the available capital cushion to absorb losses and is found by subtracting intangible assets from total bank equity capital.

insights.claim: The metric is reproducible from six public FRED balance-sheet series using the formula 100 * (a+b+c) / (d-e+f), combining nonaccrual loans, 90-plus-days-past-due loans, and other real estate owned over equity capital less intangibles plus loan-loss reserves.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
entities: Balance Sheet: Loans and Leases in Nonaccrual Status
insights.so_what: Anyone can rebuild and update this bank-stress gauge for free rather than waiting on vendor data or sell-side notes.

insights.claim: The Texas ratio was created by Gerard Cassidy of the Royal Bank of Canada to assess bank credit risk during the 1980s Texas banking crisis, whose causes included oil price shocks and real estate investments.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: The metric was purpose-built for commodity-plus-property shocks, so it is most diagnostic for banks with concentrated energy or CRE exposure rather than as a generic solvency gauge.
insights.quote: In the 1980s, Texas had a banking crisis whose causes included shocks in oil prices and real estate investments.

insights.claim: A commodity price shock transmitting into regional real estate losses is the causal chain that produced the 1980s Texas banking crisis, linking energy prices to regional bank credit quality.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Watch for the same energy-to-CRE-to-bank-capital chain in any oil-levered regional economy; the Texas ratio is the tool built to measure its end point.

themes.theme: Where US bank credit stress sits now

insights.claim: The aggregate Texas ratio for all FDIC-insured US commercial banks stands at 5.82%, near the all-time low of 4.59% set in Q2 2022, on a series running from Q1 1984 to Q1 2026.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: System-wide bank credit stress is close to its four-decade floor — an argument that any current bank-credit bear case has to rest on specific institutions or loan books, not the aggregate.
insights.quote: At the time of this writing, its value is 5.82%. That’s near the all-time low of 4.59% recorded during the second quarter of 2022.

insights.claim: A Texas ratio above 100% marks the threshold at which a bank's nonperforming loans exceed its combined tangible equity and loss reserves, signaling it may be unable to cover potential loan losses.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Gives a hard, non-arbitrary tripwire for screening individual banks; at ~5.8% aggregate, the system sits roughly 17x below that line.
insights.quote: The higher the ratio, especially if it exceeds 100%, the greater the risk of a bank being unable to cover its potential loan losses.

insights.claim: The headline aggregated Texas ratio masks dispersion by bank size, and disaggregated values by size cohort are published separately in Banking Analytics: Understanding Credit Risk with the Texas Ratio.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
entities: Banking Analytics: Understanding Credit Risk with the Texas Ratio
insights.so_what: A benign aggregate can hide a stressed small-bank tail; go to the size-cohort cut before concluding regional-bank credit is clean.
